title: Was Miyamoto Musashi Late to Ganryūjima on Purpose? Four Testimonies
description:
In 2003, Musashi's bronze statue on Ganryūjima was unveiled four months after Kojirō's, and the island's official guide leaflet joked that maybe it was to match the "historical fact" that he was late to the duel. But who was the first to say he was late on purpose?

This episode goes through the testimony one statement at a time, in the order the witnesses spoke: the stone that Musashi's adopted son Miyamoto Iori raised in Kokura in Jōō 3 (1654), nine years after Musashi's death, which says "the two heroes met at the same time"; the house record of the Numata family, castle wardens of Moji, which calls the opponent only "Kojirō"; a Kokura merchant who in Shōtoku 2 (1712) passed on what a boatman had said, written up by three generations of the Toyoda family in Kumamoto as the Bukōden of Hōreki 5 (1755) and the Nitenki of An'ei 5 (1776), which have the oversleeping, the carved oar, "Kojirō, you have lost" and the age of eighteen, but never say why he arrived late; in Meiji 42 (1909), the Miyamoto Musashi memorial society (Kenshōkai) in Kumamoto laid all the versions side by side, chose the Nitenki, and added a few lines when retelling it; the earliest text we found that writes the lateness as a ploy is a short story by Naoki Sanjūgo (Naoki died in 1934), who also recorded a criticism of unknown origin; Yoshikawa Eiji's Musashi (serialized in the Asahi Shimbun, 1935–1939) made it a story everyone knows. Last comes The Book of Five Rings, which Musashi himself began writing in Kan'ei 20 (1643).

For the Nitenki we used the text in volume 2 of the Higo Bunken Sōsho, and the memorial society's Miyamoto Musashi (which quotes the Kokura Hibun, The Book of Five Rings and the Numata Kaki); both are in the National Diet Library Digital Collections. Naoki Sanjūgo's "Ganryūjima" and Yoshikawa Eiji's novel and essays are from Aozora Bunko. We did not open the original Numata Kaki; we only used the passages quoted in the memorial society's book. For the date of the duel on Ganryūjima, the Nitenki gives the fourth month of Keichō 17 (1612); another account puts it more than ten years earlier.

The source of every quotation, year and number is listed in the references below. Dates in the narration follow the old lunar calendar, and sentences that begin "we think" are this channel's view. The guide leaflet is quoted as text only; no screenshot is shown.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. Historical figures are drawn as cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant to resemble anyone; Yoshikawa Eiji, Naoki Sanjūgo and modern researchers are not drawn.

mu101.text: April 14, 2003, on Ganryūjima: Musashi's bronze statue is unveiled.

mu103.text: The island's official guide joked: maybe it matched the "historical fact" that he was late.

mu104.text: The story we know adds a layer: he was late on purpose, to leave his rival waiting on the island.

mu105.text: But nine years after Musashi died, his son raised a stone in Kokura, recording how the two came ashore.

mu106.text: A century on, a merchant brought a boatman's words.

mu107.text: In 1909, a group in Kumamoto laid every version they could find on one table.

mu108.text: Musashi wrote a book late in life, too. How did he tell this duel?

mu109.text: So that day, was he late on purpose?

mu201.text: The first witness to that day was that stone.

mu202.text: In April 1654, Musashi's adopted son, Miyamoto Iori, set it up below Kokura Castle.

mu203.text: A devoted son raised it for posterity, it says.

mu204.text: The first witness, and the one keenest to defend him.

mu205.text: The stone's rival has no surname, no given name: just "Ganryū," a master swordsman.

mu207.text: Musashi replied: you use steel, I'll use wood.

mu208.text: Then the two came ashore. What does the stone say?

mu209.text: "The two heroes met at the same time." Both arrived together.

mu210.text: The oldest record never mentions lateness;

mu211.text: though "at the same time" may just mean both showed up, not to the minute.

mu212.text: The result is brief: one blow of the wooden sword; even lightning was slower.

mu213.text: From then on, Funashima came to be called Ganryūjima.

mu214.text: But were they the only two on the island?

mu215.text: Another is the Numata Kaki, of Moji's castle wardens.

mu216.text: As far as we found, the name "Kojirō" first appears here.

mu217.text: It began with their students arguing whose style was better.

mu218.text: It says Musashi didn't strike alone at the end; known only secondhand, that's still disputed.

mu219.text: So where did the lateness story come from?

mu301.text: The record says most details came from an old man who rowed boats.

mu302.text: Remember that merchant? In spring 1712, he came from Kokura to Yatsushiro in Higo.

mu303.text: Samurai Toyoda Masakata asked him about Ganryūjima.

mu304.text: He said a relative ran a wholesaler in Shimonoseki, where Musashi stayed;

mu305.text: an old man there had rowed Musashi's boat that day.

mu307.text: No. The book says he came many times, and told it word for word each time.

mu308.text: Three generations of the Toyoda family turned it into a book: in 1755, the Bukōden;

mu309.text: in 1776, a grandson renamed it the Nitenki.

mu310.text: This family practiced the sword style Musashi handed down.

mu311.text: How did they paint that day?

mu312.text: The book says that in April 1612, Musashi came from Kyoto to Kokura.

mu313.text: An elder's terms: Dragon hour tomorrow, on the island, Ganryū Kojirō.

mu314.text: Inspectors kept watch, under strict orders.

mu317.text: Word in town: he got scared and ran.

mu318.text: He was found in Shimonoseki, at the boatman's wholesaler.

mu319.text: The book has a letter said to be his: he won't take the elder's boat; he'll sail from here.

mu320.text: Remember one line in it: when the time is right, I'll come over.

mu321.text: Next day, the agreed hour drew near. And Musashi?

mu322.text: The sun was high, and he was still asleep.

mu323.text: Kokura's runner came twice. "Right away," he said, then washed his face and ate.

mu324.text: Remember the wooden weapon on the stone? Here, it gets a backstory:

mu325.text: He got an oar from the innkeeper and carved it into a big wooden sword ashore.

mu326.text: He reached the island past the Snake hour, two-plus hours later than agreed.

mu328.text: At the shore he yelled: "I came before the hour! Are you late?!"

mu329.text: He drew and flung the scabbard into the sea.

mu331.text: "Kojirō, you've lost. Would a winner toss his scabbard?"

mu332.text: It was decided: Kojirō lost, and Musashi bowed to the inspectors and took his boat back to Shimonoseki.

mu333.text: At the end, the stone's nameless Ganryū gets a name: Sasaki Kojirō,

mu334.text: eighteen at the time, though the book only says "it is said."

mu335.text: For all that detail, one thing is missing: why he arrived late.

mu336.text: So where were the words "on purpose" first written down?

mu401.text: Before that, the table from the start stepped in.

mu402.text: Kumamoto's Musashi memorial society was compiling Miyamoto Musashi.

mu403.text: The Numata say more than one struck at the end? The editors: not credible.

mu404.text: Remember the inspectors? The editors reasoned: orders that strict made it impossible.

mu405.text: But that reason itself comes from the Nitenki.

mu406.text: Their verdict: for now, follow the Nitenki.

mu407.text: But did they believe all of it?

mu408.text: And that "said to be eighteen" at the end? The editors admit the Nitenki's ages are unreliable.

mu409.text: An editor even crossed the sea to look for Kojirō's grave, and found no trace.

mu410.text: Stranger still, retelling that Nitenki passage, they added lines.

mu411.text: When the runner comes, this book says Kojirō is already there.

mu412.text: And Musashi? He slowly rose, calmly got to his feet, and put on a lined silk robe.

mu413.text: Kojirō's "Are you late?" became: "You broke our pact. That's too much."

mu414.text: None of this is in the Nitenki itself.

mu415.text: We think that by now, arriving late starts to look like an attitude.

mu416.text: The tone is there. But the motive?

mu501.text: What we found is a short story by Naoki Sanjūgo, who died back in 1934.

mu502.text: He followed the Nitenki, calling it reliable.

mu503.text: He wrote that as Musashi slept, he seemed to plot against Kojirō.

mu504.text: Then he quotes a criticism already going around: stalling on purpose to wear the rival down is a cowardly trick.

mu505.text: Who said it, and how early, we haven't found; Naoki himself says it may be a later voice.

mu506.text: Then he defends him: Musashi came a bit late to most bouts, on purpose, to rattle rivals.

mu507.text: Critics call it cowardly, defenders call it strategy; both are saying it was deliberate.

mu508.text: So the answer to that question: in writing that survives, this is the earliest "on purpose" we found.

mu509.text: Over a year after Naoki's death, Yoshikawa Eiji's Musashi ran four years in the Asahi.

mu511.text: In an essay, he called it the most reliable source;

mu512.text: and said Musashi's first move on Kojirō was to break the set time on purpose.

mu513.text: In the novel, the boatman warns him: it's very late now.

mu515.text: Recall the letter's "when the time is right"? Here he only says:

mu517.text: Kojirō accuses him to his face: late on purpose, every time.

mu518.text: This novel made "late on purpose" a story everyone knows.

mu519.text: But one witness in this file has said nothing all along. Who?

mu521.text: In October 1643, aged sixty, he climbed Mount Iwato in Higo and began The Book of Five Rings.

mu522.text: In the preface he counts his record: a first duel won at thirteen, another at sixteen,

mu523.text: over sixty bouts in all, never once beaten, all between thirteen and twenty-eight or nine.

mu524.text: By the Nitenki, he was twenty-nine at Ganryūjima, the end of that span.

mu526.text: In the text we checked: Ganryū, Kojirō, Funashima. Not one word.

mu527.text: The one man who'd know left nothing behind.

mu528.text: Remember the guide from the start? It also says the island back then was a sixth of its size today.

mu529.text: We think this story, like the island, grew bigger later on.

mu530.text: So "on purpose" is closed: no firsthand record gives a motive. It's a later read.

mu531.text: As for what really happened on the island, accounts still differ today.

mu533.text: Where'd you first hear "late on purpose"?

mu534.text: We only tell what's in the records. Subscribe to open files with us.
